strengths.title: Systematic comparative evaluation across multiple feature types and datasets
strengths.description: The paper provides a comprehensive comparison of four feature types (CN, CNE, LM, BoW) across five classifiers and three datasets with different languages, narrative types, and text lengths. This breadth of evaluation strengthens the empirical contribution and allows assessment of generalization.
evidence: Tables 4–7 present results for all feature-classifier combinations
Three datasets: English (Cookie Theft, 43 MCI), Portuguese (Cinderella, 20 MCI; ABCD, 23 MCI)
Five classifiers: SVM-Linear, SVM-RBF, KNN, Random Forest, Gaussian Naive Bayes
Evaluation includes individual classifiers, ensemble, and multi-view learning

strengths.title: Practical motivation and lightweight approach avoiding manual preprocessing
strengths.description: The paper addresses a real problem in neuropsychological assessment: the expense and impracticality of manual preprocessing for large-scale MCI detection. Complex networks avoid dependency on robust parsers and manual correction, making the approach more scalable and applicable to disfluent speech.
evidence: Aluísio et al. (2016) required manual revision of transcripts, removal of disfluencies, insertion of omitted subjects—expensive process
Paper eliminates lemmatization step to avoid POS tagging errors on disfluent text
No dependency or constituency parsing required
Automatic removal of filled pauses, false starts, repetitions (Cookie Theft, Cinderella)

strengths.title: Methodological innovation in applying word embedding enrichment to short texts
strengths.description: The adaptation of Perozzi et al. (2014) approach to enrich word co-occurrence networks with embedding similarity is a reasonable solution to the problem of linear networks in short texts. Figure 2 effectively demonstrates the informativeness gain from enrichment.
evidence: Figure 2 shows visual difference between co-occurrence network (a) and enriched network (b)
Justification based on Amancio (2015c): short texts have almost linear networks with little topological information
Adaptation of Perozzi et al. (2014) approach to add edges based on cosine similarity threshold
CNE generally outperforms CN across datasets (Tables 4–7)

strengths.title: Multilingual evaluation demonstrating cross-language applicability
strengths.description: The paper evaluates the approach on both English and Portuguese datasets, providing evidence of language generalization. This is valuable for demonstrating that the method is not language-specific, though some caveats apply (see concerns).
evidence: Cookie Theft: English (DementiaBank)
Cinderella and ABCD: Portuguese (University of São Paulo Medical School)
Different narrative types: picture description (Cookie Theft), story retelling (Cinderella), narrative recall (ABCD)

strengths.title: Clear presentation of methodology and transparent reporting of results
strengths.description: The paper clearly describes the network construction, feature extraction, classification algorithms, and evaluation protocol. Results are presented in detailed tables with multiple feature-classifier combinations, allowing readers to assess performance across conditions.
evidence: Section 3 clearly describes network modeling, embedding enrichment, and topological metrics
Section 4.2 details three feature types and their extraction
Section 4.3 describes classification algorithms and ensemble/multi-view strategies
Tables 4–7 present comprehensive results with all feature-classifier combinations

concerns.title: Limited algorithmic novelty; primarily application of existing techniques to new domain
concerns.description: The paper combines three established paradigms (complex networks from Amancio et al., word embeddings from Perozzi et al., multi-view learning from Collobert et al.) without substantial algorithmic innovation. The contribution is methodological (application to MCI detection) rather than advancing the underlying techniques.
evidence: Complex networks for text analysis: well-established in prior work (Amancio et al. 2012a, 2012b, 2012c, 2015a, 2015b, 2015c; de Arruda et al. 2016)
Word embedding enrichment: adapted from Perozzi et al. (2014) without modification
Multi-view learning: standard approach using majority voting (Zhou 2012; Collobert et al. 2011; Xia et al. 2011)
Topological metrics: standard graph theory measures (PageRank, Betweenness, Clustering Coefficient, etc.)
No novel ensemble strategy; majority voting is simplistic compared to weighted voting, stacking, or learned combination
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the novelty as methodological application rather than algorithmic innovation. Consider adding ablation studies or sensitivity analyses that provide new insights into when and why complex networks outperform linguistic features. Alternatively, propose domain-specific enhancements (e.g., MCI-specific topological metrics, domain-adapted embeddings).

concerns.title: Threshold tuning contradicts language-independence claim
concerns.description: The embedding similarity threshold differs between English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4), suggesting language-dependent tuning. This directly contradicts the claim that the approach is language-independent and does not require language-specific parameter optimization.
evidence: Section 5: 'threshold parameter was optimized with best values being 0.7 in Cookie Theft dataset and 0.4 in both Cinderella and ABCD dataset'
Abstract and Section 1 claim: 'language independent representation'
No justification provided for why different thresholds are optimal for different languages
Different thresholds suggest language-specific tuning is necessary, contradicting language-independence claim
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (1) provide justification for language-specific thresholds (e.g., differences in word embedding quality or semantic structure between English and Portuguese), (2) conduct sensitivity analysis showing robustness to threshold variation, or (3) revise language-independence claim to acknowledge language-dependent parameter tuning. Include ablation study varying threshold across languages to assess generalization.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported
concerns.description: Performance differences between feature types and classifiers are reported as point estimates without statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values. With small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset), differences may be within noise margin.
evidence: Tables 4–7 report accuracy as single values without confidence intervals or error bars
No statistical tests (t-test, McNemar's test, etc.) comparing feature types or classifiers
Small sample sizes: Cookie Theft 43 MCI, Cinderella 20 MCI, ABCD 23 MCI
5-fold cross-validation used, but no reporting of fold-wise variance or standard deviation
Differences between CN and CNE sometimes small (e.g., Cookie Theft SVM-RBF: 0.5694 vs 0.6264 = 5.7%)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report 95% confidence intervals for all accuracy estimates. Conduct statistical significance tests (e.g., McNemar's test for paired classifiers, paired t-tests across folds) to assess whether differences between feature types are statistically significant. Report standard deviation or standard error across folds. Consider leave-one-out cross-validation or stratified k-fold with larger k given small sample sizes.

concerns.title: Inconsistent disfluency handling across datasets complicates interpretation
concerns.description: Disfluency removal differs across datasets: Cookie Theft and Cinderella had filled pauses, false starts, and repetitions automatically removed; ABCD used automatic sentence segmentation (DeepBond). This inconsistency undermines the claim about robustness to disfluencies and makes cross-dataset comparison problematic.
evidence: Section 4.1.1 (Cookie Theft): 'automatically removed filled pauses (uh, um, er, ah), short false starts, and repetition'

Section 4.1.2 (Cinderella): 'automatically removed the disfluencies following the same guidelines of TalkBank project. However, other disfluencies (revisions, elaboration, paraphasias and comments about the task) were kept'
Section 4.1.3 (ABCD): 'used the automatic sentence segmentation method referred to as DeepBond'
No explicit comparison of performance on disfluent vs. cleaned versions of same dataset
Claim about robustness to disfluencies (Section 1, Abstract) not directly tested
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide explicit comparison of performance on disfluent vs. cleaned versions of the same dataset (e.g., Cinderella disfluent vs. Cinderella manually processed). Report which disfluencies were removed in each dataset and justify the differences. Conduct ablation study showing impact of disfluency removal on classification accuracy for each feature type.

concerns.title: Age imbalance in ABCD dataset may confound results
concerns.description: ABCD dataset shows substantial age difference between control (61 years) and MCI (72 years) groups—an 11-year gap. Age is known to affect language and cognitive performance. If age is not controlled, classifiers may learn age-related patterns rather than MCI-specific patterns.
evidence: Table 3: Control avg age 61 (SD 7.5), MCI avg age 72 (SD 7.4)
Age difference: 11 years (substantial for elderly population)
Cookie Theft and Cinderella show balanced ages (74.8 vs 73.3), but ABCD does not
No mention of age as a control variable or confound analysis
Age is known to correlate with language complexity and cognitive function
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report age as a confound variable. Conduct stratified analysis controlling for age (e.g., matched pairs, age-stratified results, or ANCOVA). Alternatively, report results separately for age-matched and age-unmatched subsets. Discuss whether age differences could explain the higher accuracy on ABCD (80%) compared to other datasets.

concerns.title: No ablation study isolating contribution of embedding enrichment
concerns.description: The paper does not provide an ablation study explicitly isolating the contribution of word embedding enrichment vs. co-occurrence alone. While Tables 4–7 show CN vs. CNE results, there is no analysis of which topological features are most discriminative or how embedding enrichment affects network topology.
evidence: Tables 4–7 show CN vs. CNE results, but no detailed analysis of differences
No reporting of which topological metrics are most important for classification
No analysis of how embedding enrichment changes network properties (e.g., density, clustering coefficient, diameter)
No comparison with alternative enrichment methods (e.g., syntactic dependencies, semantic role labels)
Figure 2 shows visual difference but no quantitative analysis of topology changes
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct ablation study varying embedding similarity threshold and reporting impact on classification accuracy. Analyze how embedding enrichment affects topological metrics (e.g., average degree, clustering coefficient, diameter) and correlate with classification performance. Use feature importance analysis (e.g., permutation importance, SHAP values) to identify which topological metrics drive classification. Compare with alternative enrichment methods.

concerns.title: Linguistic metrics pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features, biasing comparison
concerns.description: Linguistic metrics were pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features due to robustness concerns. This filtering may bias the comparison in favor of complex networks by removing potentially discriminative linguistic features, rather than demonstrating that CN is inherently superior.
evidence: Section 4.2.2: 'The metrics affected by constituency and dependency parsing were not used because they are not robust to deal with disfluencies'
Coh-Metrix for English: 106 features available, but subset used
Coh-Metrix-Dementia for Portuguese: 58 metrics used out of 73 available
Metrics based on manual annotation also discarded
This filtering removes syntactic complexity metrics, which are known to be sensitive to MCI (Roark et al. 2011, Lehr et al. 2012)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report which linguistic metrics were excluded and why. Conduct comparison using both filtered and unfiltered linguistic metrics to assess impact of filtering. Alternatively, use robust linguistic feature extraction methods that handle disfluencies (e.g., shallow parsing, chunking) instead of excluding features. Discuss whether the comparison is fair given the pre-filtering of LM features.

concerns.title: Inconsistent and modest improvements from ensemble and multi-view learning
concerns.description: Ensemble and multi-view learning improvements vary substantially across datasets (2.3% to 10%) and are sometimes inconsistent (e.g., Cinderella multi-view CNE-LM-BoW achieves 0.4750, worse than individual classifiers). This suggests the ensemble strategy may not generalize robustly.
evidence: Cookie Theft: 2.3% improvement (0.6264 → 0.65)
Cinderella: 10% improvement (0.65 → 0.75) via ensemble CNE-LM, but multi-view CNE-LM-BoW achieves 0.4750 (worse than individual classifiers)
ABCD: 4.71% improvement (0.7547 → 0.80) via multi-view CNE-LM-BoW
Majority voting is simplistic; no comparison with weighted voting, stacking, or other ensemble methods
Multi-view learning weights not explicitly reported or optimized
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report ensemble/multi-view results with confidence intervals and statistical significance tests. Conduct sensitivity analysis varying ensemble strategy (weighted voting, stacking, boosting). Report multi-view learning weights and justify their selection. Analyze why Cinderella multi-view CNE-LM-BoW performs worse than individual classifiers and whether this indicates overfitting or feature incompatibility. Compare with more sophisticated ensemble methods.

concerns.title: Word embeddings not validated for medical/dementia domain
concerns.description: Word embeddings are trained with default parameters (100 dimensions, context window 5, 5 epochs) using general-purpose corpora. No domain-specific validation or tuning is performed, which may limit the semantic quality for medical/dementia language.
evidence: Section 5: 'trained the model proposed by Bojanowski et al. (2016) with default parametrs (100 dimensional embeddings, 5 size of the context window, 5 number of epochs)'
No mention of training corpus or domain-specific tuning
No validation of embedding quality for medical/dementia language
No comparison with domain-specific embeddings (e.g., trained on medical corpora)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report the corpus used to train embeddings. Conduct domain-specific embedding training using medical or dementia-related corpora (e.g., medical literature, clinical notes). Validate embedding quality using word similarity tasks or downstream classification performance. Compare domain-specific embeddings with general-purpose embeddings to assess impact on MCI detection.

concerns.title: Small sample sizes limit statistical power and generalizability
concerns.description: Sample sizes are small (20–43 MCI per dataset), which limits statistical power for detecting true differences and raises concerns about generalizability. With 5-fold cross-validation, some folds may have only 4–8 MCI samples.
evidence: Cookie Theft: 43 MCI, 21 control (5-fold CV: ~8.6 MCI per fold)
Cinderella: 20 MCI, 20 control (5-fold CV: 4 MCI per fold)
ABCD: 23 MCI, 20 control (5-fold CV: ~4.6 MCI per fold)
Small sample sizes limit statistical power and generalizability
5-fold CV may result in high variance with such small samples
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report statistical power analysis. Consider leave-one-out cross-validation or stratified k-fold with larger k (e.g., 10-fold) to reduce variance. Report confidence intervals and standard deviations across folds. Discuss generalizability limitations. Consider combining datasets for larger sample size, or conducting external validation on independent datasets.

concerns.title: Claim of language independence contradicted by multiple language-specific design choices
concerns.description: The paper claims language independence but makes several language-specific design choices: different embedding thresholds for English vs. Portuguese, different Coh-Metrix versions, different preprocessing (manual vs. automatic segmentation), and different disfluency handling across datasets.
evidence: Abstract: 'language independent representation'
Section 1: 'language independent representation'
Threshold: 0.7 for English, 0.4 for Portuguese (Section 5)
Coh-Metrix for English (106 features), Coh-Metrix-Dementia for Portuguese (58 metrics)
Manual segmentation for Cinderella, automatic (DeepBond) for ABCD
Different disfluency handling across datasets
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Revise language-independence claim to acknowledge language-specific parameter tuning and preprocessing. Provide justification for language-specific thresholds. Conduct sensitivity analysis showing robustness to threshold variation across languages. Standardize preprocessing across datasets (manual or automatic segmentation). Discuss what aspects of the approach are truly language-independent vs. language-dependent.

concerns.title: Comparison with baselines acknowledged as not straightforward but not addressed
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges that comparison with reported baselines (60–85%) is not straightforward due to different databases and protocols, but does not conduct any head-to-head comparison or address this limitation substantively.
evidence: Section 6: 'The comparison with our results is not straightforward, though, because the databases used in the studies are different'
Baseline studies use different datasets (WLM, Picnic, animated films) not directly comparable to Cookie Theft, Cinderella, ABCD
No attempt to re-implement baselines on the same datasets
No discussion of how differences in datasets, evaluation protocols, or feature engineering affect comparison
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct head-to-head comparison with at least one baseline method on the same dataset (e.g., re-implement Aluísio et al. 2016 on Cinderella dataset). Alternatively, provide detailed analysis of how dataset differences, evaluation protocols, and feature engineering affect performance comparison. Discuss whether the 60–85% baseline range is appropriate for comparison.

concerns.title: No analysis of which topological features are most discriminative
concerns.description: The paper extracts 30 topological features (10 metrics × 3 statistics: average, standard deviation, skewness) but does not analyze which features are most important for MCI classification. This limits interpretability and understanding of what network properties distinguish MCI from controls.
evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'ten measurements' with 'average μ(X), standard deviation σ(X) and skewness γ(X) for each measurement'
No feature importance analysis (e.g., permutation importance, SHAP values, correlation with MCI status)
No discussion of which topological properties are most discriminative
No interpretation of what network properties distinguish MCI from controls
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct feature importance analysis using permutation importance, SHAP values, or correlation analysis. Report which topological metrics are most discriminative for MCI detection. Discuss what these metrics reveal about language changes in MCI (e.g., reduced network connectivity, altered clustering patterns). Provide interpretable insights into how complex networks capture MCI-related language impairment.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on complex networks for NLP tasks (text classification, summarization, authorship detection, literary movement identification)
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper directly builds on Amancio's work by applying complex network topological metrics to MCI detection. The novelty is in the application domain (neuropsychological assessment) rather than in the network methodology itself. Amancio's work on short texts (2015c) directly motivates the embedding enrichment approach.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper adapts Perozzi et al.'s approach to enrich word co-occurrence networks with embedding similarity. The adaptation is straightforward (adding edges based on cosine similarity threshold) with no substantial modification. The novelty is in applying this technique to short medical texts.

Aluísio et al. required manual preprocessing (removal of disfluencies, insertion of omitted subjects); this paper avoids manual preprocessing using complex networks. However, the comparison is complicated by different feature types and preprocessing approaches.

comparable_works.citation_label: Roark et al. (2011), Lehr et al. (2012), Tóth et al. (2015), Vincze et al. (2016)

Threshold selection (0.7 vs. 0.4) differs between English and Portuguese, contradicting language-independence claim; no justification provided

No ablation study isolating contribution of embedding enrichment vs. co-occurrence alone; no analysis of which topological features are most discriminative
Comparison with baselines (60–85%) acknowledged as not straightforward due to different databases; no head-to-head comparison on same datasets
Multi-view learning weights not explicitly reported or optimized; unclear how feature spaces are combined
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for performance differences; differences may be within noise margin
Generalization to other languages, assessment types, or MCI subtypes not addressed; limited to three datasets from two languages
alternative_interpretations: The superior performance of CNE vs. LM may reflect the pre-filtering of linguistic metrics (removal of parser-dependent features) rather than inherent superiority of complex networks. A fair comparison would use robust linguistic feature extraction methods.

The improvement from ensemble and multi-view learning may be driven by BoW features rather than complex networks. In ABCD, SVM-Linear BoW alone achieves 0.7547, close to the multi-view result of 0.80, suggesting BoW may be the primary contributor.

The language-independence claim may be overstated. The different thresholds for English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4) suggest language-dependent tuning is necessary, and the use of language-specific Coh-Metrix versions and preprocessing approaches undermines the language-independence narrative.

The robustness to disfluencies claim may be misleading. Disfluencies were partially removed (filled pauses, false starts, repetitions), and the Cinderella manually processed version (Table 6) shows that linguistic metrics actually improve on cleaned data (0.7250 vs. 0.4750), suggesting that disfluencies may be diagnostic markers that should be preserved rather than removed.

The modest improvements (2.3–10%) and inconsistency across datasets may indicate that the approach does not generalize robustly. The improvements could be dataset-specific artifacts rather than evidence of a generalizable method.

The claim that complex networks avoid manual preprocessing may be overstated. The approach still requires tokenization, stopword removal, and sentence segmentation (manual for Cinderella, automatic for ABCD), which are language-specific preprocessing steps.
transparency_notes: This review is based on the incremental-contribution lens, which evaluates how the paper extends, refines, or reorganizes existing paradigms. The paper combines three established techniques (complex networks, word embeddings, multi-view learning) in a novel application domain (MCI detection), which constitutes incremental but meaningful progress.

The retrieved literature corpus did not return papers directly comparable to this work (e.g., other applications of embedding-enriched networks to medical NLP). This may reflect sparse coverage of this specific combination in the indexed corpus, not necessarily a lack of prior work.

The novelty assessment is complicated by the tension between methodological innovation (application to MCI detection) and algorithmic innovation (limited). The paper makes a practical contribution by avoiding manual preprocessing, but this is more of an engineering contribution than a scientific innovation.

The uncertainty flags and concerns are substantial, particularly regarding statistical testing, small sample sizes, and contradictions between claims (language-independence) and evidence (language-specific thresholds). These issues should be addressed before publication.

The paper's strengths lie in systematic evaluation and practical motivation, but weaknesses in statistical rigor and claim substantiation are significant. The incremental nature of the contribution, combined with methodological concerns, suggests this work is suitable for a specialized venue (e.g., workshop, domain-specific conference) rather than a top-tier general NLP conference.

The creativity safeguard analysis suggests the work has some innovation signal (application of embedding-enriched networks to MCI detection), but the signal is moderate rather than strong. The lack of close analogs in the corpus could indicate novelty, but it could also reflect the specialized nature of the application domain.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The absence of close analogs in the retrieved literature corpus suggests the specific combination of embedding-enriched networks for MCI detection is novel. However, novelty does not guarantee validity or impact. The paper's methodological flaws (lack of statistical testing, small sample sizes, contradictory claims) and modest empirical improvements (2.3–10%) raise questions about the practical significance of the contribution.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the paper provided statistical significance testing and confidence intervals, the claimed improvements would be more credible and interpretable.
If the paper conducted head-to-head comparison with at least one baseline method on the same dataset, the comparison with the 60–85% baseline range would be more meaningful.

If the paper provided ablation studies isolating the contribution of embedding enrichment and analyzing which topological features are most discriminative, the mechanistic understanding of why complex networks work would be clearer.
If the paper addressed the language-independence contradiction (different thresholds for different languages) with sensitivity analysis or justification, the claim would be more credible.
If the paper controlled for age as a confound variable in ABCD and reported results stratified by age, the validity of the ABCD results would be strengthened.
If the paper used domain-specific word embeddings (trained on medical corpora) and validated their quality, the semantic enrichment would be more appropriate for medical language.
If the paper compared more sophisticated ensemble methods (weighted voting, stacking, boosting) with majority voting, the ensemble contribution would be better understood.
If the paper reported multi-view learning weights and justified their selection, the multi-view learning approach would be more transparent and reproducible.

The empirical contribution is systematic evaluation on three multilingual datasets, but with modest improvements (2.3–10%) and methodological concerns (no statistical testing, small sample sizes, contradictory claims).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes enriching word co-occurrence networks with word embeddings to detect mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from speech transcripts, evaluated on three multilingual datasets. The core novelty claim is that complex network (CN) topological features outperform traditional linguistic metrics without requiring manual preprocessing or robust parsers. The approach combines three feature types (CN, linguistic metrics, bag-of-words) via ensemble and multi-view learning. While the application of embedding-enriched networks to MCI detection is novel in the specific domain, the underlying methodological components (word adjacency networks, word embeddings, ensemble learning) are well-established. The paper's contribution is primarily in application and empirical validation rather than conceptual innovation. However, the motivation to avoid parser-dependent feature extraction in disfluent speech is pragmatically sound and addresses a real clinical bottleneck. Critical concerns include small sample sizes, lack of statistical significance testing, inconsistent language-dependent design choices (threshold tuning), and limited ablation analysis. The paper demonstrates competitive performance (65–80% accuracy) within reported baseline ranges but does not establish clear superiority or mechanistic understanding of why topological features work.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: MCI detection via linguistic analysis is clinically valuable for early diagnosis.
Premise 2: Traditional linguistic feature extraction depends on robust parsers and manual preprocessing.
Premise 3: Disfluent speech in MCI patients degrades parser performance, making manual correction expensive and non-scalable.
Premise 4: Complex networks (word adjacency graphs) are lightweight, language-independent, and do not require parsing.
Premise 5: Short texts produce linear networks with low topological informativeness (Amancio 2015c).
Premise 6: Word embeddings capture semantic similarity and can enrich sparse networks with additional edges.
Conclusion A (Main Claim): Enriching co-occurrence networks with word embedding similarity improves classification on short texts.
Conclusion B (Comparative Claim): Complex network features outperform traditional linguistic metrics for MCI detection.
Conclusion C (Ensemble Claim): Combining heterogeneous feature spaces via ensemble and multi-view learning improves accuracy.
Conclusion D (Practical Claim): The approach is language-independent and requires no manual preprocessing.
Critical Tension: Thresholds differ between English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4), contradicting language-independence claim.
Critical Tension: Linguistic metrics were pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features, potentially biasing comparison in favor of CN.
Critical Tension: Disfluency handling is inconsistent across datasets (some removed, others kept), undermining robustness claim.
Critical Tension: Small sample sizes and lack of statistical significance testing limit confidence in performance differences.

strengths.title: Pragmatic motivation addressing real clinical bottleneck
strengths.description: The paper identifies a genuine problem: manual preprocessing and parser-dependent feature extraction are expensive and error-prone for disfluent clinical speech. The motivation to develop an automated, lightweight alternative is clinically relevant and addresses a scalability concern in neuropsychological assessment.
evidence: Aluísio et al. (2016) required manual revision, removal of disfluencies, insertion of omitted subjects—expensive process
Paper explicitly states: 'manually correcting transcripts of patient's speech is not a solution to large scale assessments'
Complex networks avoid dependency on POS tagging and parsing, reducing error propagation in disfluent text

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three multilingual datasets
strengths.description: The paper evaluates the approach on three datasets with different languages (English, Portuguese), narrative types (Cookie Theft, Cinderella, ABCD), and text lengths. This breadth of evaluation demonstrates effort to assess generalization across contexts.
evidence: Cookie Theft: English, short descriptions, 43 MCI + 43 control
Cinderella: Portuguese, longer narratives, 20 MCI + 20 control
ABCD: Portuguese, very short narratives, 23 MCI + 20 control
Systematic comparison of CN, CNE, LM, BoW features across five classifiers

strengths.description: The adaptation of Perozzi et al. (2014) to enrich sparse co-occurrence networks with semantic similarity is a reasonable response to the known problem that short texts produce linear networks with low topological informativeness. The intuition is sound: adding edges based on semantic similarity can increase network density and informativeness.

Figure 2 visually demonstrates that enriched network (b) is more informative than linear network (a)
Adaptation of Perozzi et al. (2014) approach is methodologically coherent

strengths.title: Competitive classification performance within baseline ranges
strengths.description: The reported accuracies (65–80%) fall within the reported baseline range of 60–85%, suggesting the approach achieves competitive performance. The 80% accuracy on ABCD is at the upper end of the baseline range.

Cinderella: 75% (ensemble CNE-LM)
ABCD: 80% (multi-view CNE-LM-BoW)
Baseline range: 60–85% from prior work

strengths.description: The paper provides detailed demographic information (age, education, gender) for all three datasets and clearly describes inclusion/exclusion criteria and diagnostic procedures. This transparency aids reproducibility and allows assessment of potential confounds.
evidence: Tables 1–3 provide comprehensive demographic data
Cookie Theft: inclusion criteria specified (age >44, education ≥7 years, MMSE ≥10)
Cinderella and ABCD: diagnosed by multidisciplinary team with explicit consensus criteria
Detailed description of narrative elicitation procedures for each dataset

strengths.title: Systematic comparison of multiple feature types and classifiers
strengths.description: The paper compares four feature types (CN, CNE, LM, BoW) across five classifiers (SVM-Linear, SVM-RBF, KNN, RF, Gaussian NB) and three datasets. This systematic comparison provides useful empirical evidence about relative performance.
evidence: Tables 4–7 show results for all combinations of feature types and classifiers
Ensemble and multi-view learning strategies tested
Consistent reporting format across datasets

concerns.title: Lack of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals
concerns.description: No statistical significance tests (t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, permutation tests) or confidence intervals are reported for any performance comparisons. With small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset), this is a critical omission. Performance differences may be within noise margins.
evidence: All results reported as point estimates without error bars or confidence intervals
No p-values or statistical tests reported for any claim
Small sample sizes: Cookie Theft 43 MCI, Cinderella 20 MCI, ABCD 23 MCI
5-fold cross-validation used, but no variance estimates reported
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-tests on fold-level accuracies, permutation tests) and report 95% confidence intervals for all performance metrics. Use stratified k-fold CV with larger k (e.g., 10-fold) or leave-one-out CV for more stable estimates on small datasets.

concerns.title: Language-dependent threshold tuning contradicts language-independence claim
concerns.description: The embedding similarity threshold differs between English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4), indicating language-dependent tuning. This directly contradicts the claim that the approach is 'language-independent' and does not require language-specific parameter tuning.
evidence: Section 5: 'threshold parameter was optimized with best values being 0.7 in Cookie Theft dataset and 0.4 in both Cinderella and ABCD dataset'
Abstract claims: 'language independent representation'
Section 1 claims: 'does not require manual transcript correction or robust dependency/constituency parsers'
No justification provided for why thresholds differ by language
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (1) identify a language-independent threshold that works across datasets and report performance with that fixed threshold, or (2) revise the language-independence claim to acknowledge that threshold tuning is required per language. Provide ablation study showing sensitivity to threshold across languages.

concerns.title: Biased comparison: linguistic metrics pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features
concerns.description: Linguistic metrics were pre-filtered to exclude features that depend on parsing (constituency, dependency). This creates an unfair comparison: complex networks are compared against a weakened version of linguistic features, not against the full potential of linguistic approaches.
evidence: Section 4.2.2: 'The metrics affected by constituency and dependency parsing were not used because they are not robust to deal with disfluencies.'
Coh-Metrix provides 106 features for English; only a subset used
Coh-Metrix-Dementia provides 73 metrics; only 58 used
This filtering was done to avoid parser errors, but it weakens the linguistic baseline
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results with both (1) filtered linguistic metrics (current approach) and (2) full linguistic metrics to show the true performance gap. Alternatively, use robust parsing methods (e.g., neural dependency parsers) that may handle disfluencies better. Discuss this limitation explicitly in the paper.

concerns.title: No ablation study isolating embedding enrichment contribution
concerns.description: The paper does not isolate the contribution of word embedding enrichment. Tables 4–7 show CN vs. CNE, but there is no controlled ablation varying only the enrichment step while holding other factors constant. The improvement from enrichment could be due to other factors (e.g., threshold optimization, classifier tuning).
evidence: Tables 4–7 show CN and CNE results, but no systematic ablation
No analysis of which topological features are most discriminative
No sensitivity analysis for threshold parameter
Claim C2 ('enriching networks improves performance') lacks direct evidence
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct ablation study: (1) co-occurrence network alone, (2) co-occurrence + embedding enrichment with threshold T, (3) embedding enrichment with different thresholds. Report performance for each variant. Analyze which topological features contribute most to classification.

concerns.title: Inconsistent disfluency handling across datasets undermines robustness claim
concerns.description: Disfluency handling differs across datasets: Cookie Theft and Cinderella had some disfluencies automatically removed (filled pauses, false starts, repetitions), while others were kept (revisions, paraphasias). ABCD used automatic segmentation (DeepBond). This inconsistency undermines the claim that the approach is robust to disfluencies.
evidence: Cookie Theft: 'automatically removed filled pauses (uh, um, er, ah), short false starts, and repetition'
Cinderella: 'automatically removed disfluencies following TalkBank guidelines, but kept revisions, elaborations, paraphasias, and task comments'
ABCD: 'used automatic sentence segmentation method referred to as DeepBond'
No explicit comparison of performance on disfluent vs. cleaned versions of same dataset
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct controlled experiment: (1) evaluate on original disfluent transcripts, (2) evaluate on cleaned transcripts with disfluencies removed, (3) report performance difference. This directly tests robustness to disfluencies. Standardize disfluency handling across all datasets.

concerns.title: Age imbalance in ABCD dataset may confound results
concerns.description: The ABCD dataset shows an 11-year age difference between control (mean 61) and MCI (mean 72) groups. Age is known to affect language and cognitive performance. If age is not controlled, classifiers may learn age-related patterns rather than MCI-specific patterns.
evidence: Table 3: Control avg age 61 (SD 7.5), MCI avg age 72 (SD 7.4)
Age difference: 11 years, substantial
No mention of age as a control variable or covariate in analysis
No stratified results by age group
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results stratified by age group or use age as a covariate in classification models. Conduct analysis to assess whether age is a confound. Consider matching control and MCI groups on age, or report results separately for age-matched and age-unmatched subsets.

concerns.title: Simplistic ensemble strategy without comparison to alternatives
concerns.description: The ensemble strategy uses majority voting, which treats all classifiers equally. No comparison with weighted voting, stacking, or other ensemble methods. Multi-view learning weights are not explicitly reported or optimized.
evidence: Section 4.3: 'multiple models/classifiers are generated and combined using, e.g. majority vote or average of class probabilities'
Tables 4–7: only majority voting results reported
No discussion of how weights are assigned in multi-view learning
No comparison with other ensemble methods
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compare majority voting with weighted voting, stacking, or other ensemble methods. Report learned weights for multi-view learning. Conduct sensitivity analysis for ensemble strategy. Justify choice of majority voting.

concerns.title: Word embeddings not validated for medical/dementia domain
concerns.description: Word embeddings are trained with default parameters (100 dimensions, context window 5, 5 epochs) on unspecified corpus. No validation that these embeddings capture domain-specific semantic relationships relevant to dementia-related language.
evidence: Section 5: 'trained the model proposed by Bojanowski et al. (2016) with default parametrs (100 dimensional embeddings, 5 size of the context window, 5 number of epochs)'
No mention of training corpus or domain-specific tuning
No analysis of embedding quality or semantic capture in medical domain
No comparison with domain-specific embeddings (e.g., trained on medical corpora)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report training corpus for embeddings. Validate embeddings on medical/dementia-related word similarity tasks. Compare with domain-specific embeddings trained on clinical corpora. Conduct sensitivity analysis for embedding dimensionality and context window.

concerns.title: Inconsistent improvement from ensemble/multi-view learning across datasets
concerns.description: Improvement from ensemble and multi-view learning varies substantially across datasets (2.3% to 10%), suggesting the method may not generalize robustly. In some cases (Table 5), ensemble performs worse than individual classifiers.
evidence: Cookie Theft: 2.3% improvement (0.65 vs 0.6264)
Cinderella: 10% improvement (0.75 vs 0.65)
ABCD: 4.71% improvement (0.80 vs 0.7547)
Table 5: ensemble 0.6000 vs CNE 0.6500 (ensemble worse than individual)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze why ensemble/multi-view learning works better on some datasets than others. Investigate dataset-specific factors (text length, narrative type, language) that affect ensemble performance. Provide guidance on when ensemble methods are beneficial.

concerns.title: No analysis of which topological features drive classification
concerns.description: The paper extracts 30 topological features (10 metrics × 3 statistics: mean, std, skewness) but treats them as a black box. No feature importance analysis, feature selection, or interpretation of which features are most discriminative for MCI detection.
evidence: Section 4.2.1: lists 10 topological measurements, then calculates mean, std, skewness for each
No feature importance analysis (e.g., permutation importance, SHAP values)
No feature selection or dimensionality reduction
No interpretation of which features are most predictive of MCI
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct feature importance analysis to identify which topological features are most discriminative. Use feature selection (e.g., recursive feature elimination) to reduce dimensionality. Provide interpretation of why certain topological features are informative for MCI detection.

concerns.title: Limited novelty in underlying methodological components
concerns.description: The paper combines three well-established techniques (word adjacency networks, word embeddings, ensemble learning) in a new application domain (MCI detection). While the application is novel, the methodological components are not. The contribution is primarily empirical validation rather than conceptual innovation.
evidence: Word adjacency networks: established since Cancho & Solé (2001), applied to text classification by de Arruda et al. (2016)
Word embeddings: standard technique (Bojanowski et al. 2016)
Ensemble learning: standard technique (Zhou 2012)
Perozzi et al. (2014) already proposed enriching networks with embeddings
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the novelty contribution: is it (1) application of existing methods to MCI detection, (2) methodological innovation in network enrichment, or (3) empirical findings about feature effectiveness? Frame contribution appropriately. Consider whether methodological innovation is needed or if application-level contribution is sufficient.

concerns.title: Sparse precedent in applying embedding-enriched networks to clinical NLP
concerns.description: While word adjacency networks and word embeddings are well-established, their combination for clinical speech analysis (specifically MCI detection) appears to be novel. The paper does not cite prior work applying embedding-enriched networks to clinical or neuropsychological assessment.
evidence: Perozzi et al. (2014) proposed enriching networks with embeddings, but for general NLP tasks
No prior work cited applying this approach to MCI or dementia detection
Application to disfluent clinical speech is novel
Motivation to avoid parser-dependent feature extraction in clinical context is underexplored in prior work
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct more thorough literature review of clinical NLP and neuropsychological assessment to identify any prior work on network-based or embedding-based approaches. Clarify what is truly novel about the application.

concerns.title: Generalization concerns: limited assessment types and languages
concerns.description: The paper evaluates on three datasets, but all use similar narrative/description tasks (Cookie Theft, Cinderella, ABCD). Generalization to other assessment types (e.g., fluency tasks, conversation, reading) or languages beyond English and Portuguese is unclear.
evidence: All three datasets use narrative or description tasks
Only two languages: English and Portuguese
No evaluation on other dementia types (AD, vascular dementia, etc.)

alternative_interpretations: The superior performance of CNE over LM may not reflect the true potential of linguistic approaches, but rather the biased comparison (LM pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features). A fair comparison would use robust parsing methods or full linguistic metrics.
The improvement from embedding enrichment may be due to threshold optimization or classifier tuning rather than the enrichment itself. An ablation study would clarify this.

The inconsistent improvement from ensemble/multi-view learning across datasets suggests the method may be dataset-specific rather than generally applicable. The approach may work well for longer narratives (Cinderella) but less well for short descriptions (Cookie Theft, ABCD).

The claim of 'language-independence' may be overstated. The language-dependent threshold tuning suggests the approach requires language-specific parameter optimization, which is a form of language-dependence.

The robustness to disfluencies may be overstated. The paper partially removes disfluencies (filled pauses, false starts) but keeps others (revisions, paraphasias). The approach may not be truly robust to all types of disfluencies.

The competitive performance (65–80% accuracy) may not represent a significant advance over baselines. The baseline range (60–85%) is wide, and the paper's results fall within this range without clear superiority.

The motivation to avoid manual preprocessing may be less compelling than presented. Modern neural dependency parsers (e.g., Stanza) are more robust to disfluencies than traditional parsers, potentially reducing the need for manual correction.

The paper would benefit from clearer framing of what is truly novel: is it the application, the methodological combination, or the empirical findings? The methodological concerns (lack of statistical testing, biased comparison, inconsistent design) are significant but addressable and do not negate the novelty of the application.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents a novel application with pragmatic motivation and reasonable methodological design, but is hampered by significant methodological concerns (lack of statistical testing, biased comparison, inconsistent design choices, small sample sizes). The novelty is primarily in application rather than methodology, and the empirical findings are competitive but not clearly superior to baselines. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes enriching word co-occurrence networks with word embeddings to detect mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from speech transcripts, evaluated on three multilingual datasets (English DementiaBank Cookie Theft, Portuguese Cinderella, Portuguese ABCD). The core claims are: (1) complex network (CN) features outperform traditional linguistic metrics (LM) across all datasets; (2) word embedding enrichment improves network informativeness on short texts; (3) ensemble and multi-view learning achieve substantial improvements (10% on Cinderella, 4.71% on ABCD); (4) the approach is robust to disfluencies and language-independent. As a claim verifier operating in evidence-and-uncertainty-first mode, I reconstruct the paper's logical argument and cross-check each claim against manuscript evidence, prior reviewer digests, and retrieved literature. The analysis reveals a pattern of partially supported claims with significant evidentiary gaps: performance differences lack statistical significance testing; threshold selection contradicts language-independence claims; disfluency robustness is asserted but not directly tested; linguistic metrics baseline is potentially biased by pre-filtering parser-dependent features; and small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) undermine generalizability. The paper's core methodological contribution—enriching networks with embeddings—is sound and novel in application, but empirical validation is underdeveloped. Claims about superiority and robustness are overstated relative to available evidence.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Linguistic feature extraction depends on robust parsers (supported by Aluísio et al. 2016 example)
Premise 2: MCI disfluencies produce agrammatical speech that breaks parsers (asserted, not directly tested)
Premise 3: Complex networks avoid parser dependency via word adjacency (supported by methodology)
Premise 4: Short texts produce uninformative linear networks (supported by Amancio 2015c citation)
Premise 5: Word embedding enrichment adds semantic edges to networks (supported by Perozzi et al. 2014 adaptation)
Conclusion A: Enriched networks (CNE) should outperform linguistic metrics (LM) → Claim C1
Evidence for A: Tables 4–7 show CNE > LM in most cases, but no significance testing; LM pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features (potential bias)
Conclusion B: Ensemble and multi-view learning combine heterogeneous features effectively → Claim C3
Evidence for B: Cinderella 75% (10% improvement), ABCD 80% (4.71% improvement), but Cookie Theft only 2.3% improvement; inconsistency suggests limited robustness
Conclusion C: Approach is language-independent and requires no manual preprocessing → Claim C5

Evidence for C: Applied to English and Portuguese, no lemmatization required, but threshold tuning differs (0.7 vs 0.4), contradicting language-independence; manual sentence segmentation in Cinderella; different Coh-Metrix versions for different languages
Conclusion D: Approach is robust to disfluencies → Claim C4
Evidence for D: Disfluencies partially removed (filled pauses, false starts) but others kept (revisions, paraphasias); no explicit comparison of disfluent vs. cleaned versions on same dataset

Language-dependent threshold tuning (0.7 vs 0.4) could reflect genuine linguistic differences between English and Portuguese rather than method limitation. Alternative interpretation: approach is language-aware rather than language-independent; tuning is necessary and acceptable.

Pre-filtering of LM features could be justified as fair comparison (both methods avoid parser-dependent features). Alternative interpretation: comparison is fair because both methods use robust features; filtering is necessary for disfluent data.

transparency_notes: This review operates in evidence-and-uncertainty-first mode, prioritizing explicit documentation of evidentiary gaps and alternative interpretations over binary verdicts.

Claim verification is based on manuscript evidence, prior reviewer digests, and retrieved literature. Absence of evidence in retrieved literature does not imply invalidity; it may reflect sparse coverage or indexing gaps.
Retrieved literature corpus (Q1/Q2 articles) is limited; absence of close matches does not indicate lack of precedent in broader literature.
Reviewer guidelines retrieved are general ACL/NLP standards; field-specific standards for clinical NLP or neuropsychological assessment may differ.
Small sample sizes and lack of statistical testing create high uncertainty in performance comparisons. Confidence intervals for all claims are wide.

Prior reviewer digests (reviewers 1–4) provide consistent identification of key concerns (statistical testing, threshold justification, bias in comparison, disfluency testing). This review synthesizes and deepens those concerns.
Novelty assessment is separate from validity assessment. Methodological flaws do not necessarily indicate lack of novelty; conversely, novelty does not excuse methodological gaps.
Counterfactual reasoning applied: under what conditions could claims be valid? (See creativity_safeguard section.)
This review does not recommend accept/reject; it documents strengths, concerns, and uncertainty to inform editorial decision-making.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The application of embedding-enriched complex networks to MCI detection is novel in the specific domain (neuropsychological assessment) and represents a meaningful methodological contribution. However, novelty does not excuse methodological gaps (lack of statistical testing, biased comparison, incomplete ablation). The core innovation—adapting Perozzi et al. (2014) to short texts for MCI detection—is sound but empirically underdeveloped.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If statistical significance testing were conducted and differences remained significant (p < 0.05), claim C1 would be substantially strengthened.
If threshold selection were justified via sensitivity analysis and shown to be robust across languages, language-independence claim (C5) would be credible.
If disfluency robustness were directly tested via explicit comparison of disfluent vs. cleaned versions on same dataset, claim C4 would be supported.
If linguistic metrics were compared fairly (without pre-filtering parser-dependent features), claim C1 would be more convincing. Table 6 result suggests LM may outperform CN on clean data.
If ensemble improvements were consistent across datasets (not just 2.3% to 10% variation), claim C3 would be more robust.
If domain-specific embeddings were used and compared with general-purpose embeddings, the contribution would be stronger.
If feature importance analysis were conducted, the paper would provide interpretability and mechanistic understanding of why topological features work.
If sample sizes were larger (100+ MCI per dataset) or statistical power were demonstrated, generalizability claims would be justified.
If the paper acknowledged limitations (small sample sizes, lack of significance testing, biased comparison) and positioned results as preliminary, credibility would increase.

The paper provides systematic comparative evaluation across four feature types (CN, CNE, LM, BoW), five classifiers, and three datasets with different languages and narrative types

Novelty assessment: reviewers 3-4 differ on whether application-level contribution (MCI detection) constitutes meaningful novelty vs. incremental application of established techniques
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical significance of performance differences: No significance testing reported; with small sample sizes (20-43 MCI per dataset) and 5-fold CV, differences may be within noise margins. Confidence intervals for all accuracy claims are wide and unquantified.

Threshold selection justification: Different thresholds for English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4) lack justification. No sensitivity analysis provided. Unclear whether thresholds were optimized on test set (potential overfitting) or validation set.

Linguistic metrics baseline fairness: LM features pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent metrics, while CN features use all topological measures. Comparison may be asymmetric. Table 6 shows LM outperforms CNE on manually cleaned Cinderella (0.7250 vs 0.6500), contradicting main claim.

Disfluency robustness: Claim asserts robustness but disfluencies were partially removed (filled pauses, false starts) rather than fully preserved. No explicit comparison of disfluent vs. cleaned versions on same dataset. Inconsistent disfluency handling across datasets (manual segmentation in Cinderella, automatic in ABCD).

Age confound in ABCD: 11-year age difference between control (61) and MCI (72) groups. Age is known to affect language and cognitive performance. No stratified analysis or age-matching reported. Unclear whether high accuracy (80%) reflects MCI-specific patterns or age-related differences.

Embedding domain validation: Word embeddings trained with default parameters (Bojanowski et al. 2016) without domain-specific tuning or validation for medical/dementia language. No comparison with domain-specific embeddings.

Ensemble strategy robustness: Improvements inconsistent across datasets (2.3% to 10%). Majority voting is simplistic; no comparison with weighted voting or stacking. Multi-view learning weights not explicitly reported or optimized.

Generalization scope: Evaluation limited to three datasets, two languages (English, Portuguese), and similar narrative tasks (Cookie Theft, Cinderella, ABCD). Generalization to other languages, assessment types, or MCI subtypes unclear.

meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a novel application of embedding-enriched complex networks to MCI detection with pragmatic motivation and systematic evaluation, but exhibits significant methodological gaps that prevent strong conclusions. Core concerns: (1) Absence of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals undermines all performance claims; with small sample sizes (20-43 MCI per dataset), reported differences may be within noise margins. (2) Linguistic metrics baseline is weakened by pre-filtering parser-dependent features, creating asymmetric comparison. Table 6 result (LM 0.7250 vs CNE 0.6500 on clean Cinderella) contradicts main claim. (3) Language-dependent threshold tuning (0.7 vs 0.4) directly contradicts language-independence claim; no justification provided. (4) Disfluency robustness is asserted but not directly tested; disfluencies were partially removed rather than fully preserved. (5) Age imbalance in ABCD dataset (11-year difference) may confound results; no stratified analysis. (6) Ensemble improvements are inconsistent across datasets (2.3-10%), suggesting limited robustness. Recommendation: Desk reject or major revision required. If revision path is chosen, require: (a) statistical significance testing with confidence intervals for all claims; (b) fair comparison with linguistic metrics (either full feature set or equivalent filtering); (c) sensitivity analysis for threshold selection across languages; (d) explicit disfluency robustness testing (disfluent vs. cleaned versions); (e) age-stratified analysis for ABCD; (f) feature importance analysis to provide mechanistic understanding. The paper's practical motivation and systematic evaluation are strengths, but methodological rigor must be substantially improved before publication.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper addresses a genuine clinical problem and proposes a reasonable methodological approach, but empirical validation is underdeveloped. To strengthen the work: (1) Conduct statistical significance testing (paired t-tests, McNemar's test) for all performance comparisons. Report 95% confidence intervals for all accuracy values. With small sample sizes, consider leave-one-out CV or stratified k-fold with larger k. (2) Provide fair comparison with linguistic metrics: either use full Coh-Metrix feature sets without pre-filtering, or apply equivalent filtering to both CN and LM features. Explain why Table 6 shows LM outperforming CNE on clean Cinderella data (0.7250 vs 0.6500). (3) Justify threshold selection: provide sensitivity analysis showing accuracy across threshold range (0.1-0.9) for both English and Portuguese. Explain why different thresholds are optimal for different languages, or demonstrate that language-independent threshold works equally well. (4) Directly test disfluency robustness: evaluate on both disfluent and cleaned versions of same dataset (e.g., Cinderella). Report results separately for each version. Analyze which disfluency types most affect each feature type. (5) Address age confound in ABCD: report results stratified by age group or use age-matched control group. Include age as covariate in classification model. (6) Validate word embeddings for medical/dementia domain: compare general-purpose embeddings with domain-specific embeddings trained on medical corpora. (7) Conduct ablation study isolating contribution of embedding enrichment: vary threshold, compare with alternative enrichment methods, analyze which topological features benefit most from enrichment. (8) Analyze ensemble robustness: investigate why improvements vary across datasets (2.3-10%). Compare majority voting with weighted voting and stacking. Report multi-view learning weights explicitly. (9) Provide feature importance analysis: identify which topological metrics are most discriminative for MCI detection. Interpret findings in terms of language/cognitive properties. (10) Revise claims to match evidence: acknowledge language-dependent parameter tuning; frame as 'language-adaptable' rather than 'language-independent'. Acknowledge that disfluency handling is partial rather than complete. Clarify that ensemble improvements are inconsistent across datasets.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes enriching word co-occurrence networks with word embeddings to detect mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from speech transcripts, evaluated on three multilingual datasets (English DementiaBank Cookie Theft, Portuguese Cinderella, Portuguese ABCD). The core contribution is methodological—adapting Perozzi et al. (2014) embedding enrichment to address the problem of short texts producing uninformative linear networks—combined with systematic empirical evaluation across four feature types, five classifiers, and three datasets. The paper reports competitive classification performance (65–80% accuracy) within established baseline ranges (60–85%) and demonstrates that ensemble and multi-view learning strategies can improve individual classifier results. The practical motivation is sound: avoiding manual preprocessing and parser-dependent feature extraction for disfluent clinical speech. However, the paper exhibits significant methodological gaps that prevent strong conclusions: absence of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals; biased comparison between complex network (CN) and linguistic metric (LM) features due to pre-filtering of parser-dependent LM metrics; language-dependent threshold tuning (0.7 for English, 0.4 for Portuguese) contradicting language-independence claims; disfluency robustness asserted but not directly tested; and small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) limiting generalizability. Five specialist reviewers operating under different cognitive roles (structure analyst, methodology auditor, incremental novelty assessor, disruptive novelty assessor, claim verifier) converge on identifying these gaps while disagreeing on severity and implications. The paper makes an incremental but meaningful contribution to clinical NLP by demonstrating that embedding-enriched networks can be competitive with linguistic approaches for MCI detection, but empirical validation is underdeveloped and several key claims are overstated relative to available evidence.
strengths: Pragmatic motivation addressing genuine clinical bottleneck: The paper identifies a real problem in neuropsychological assessment—the expense and impracticality of manual preprocessing for large-scale MCI detection—and proposes a lightweight, parser-free alternative grounded in prior work (Aluísio et al. 2016).

Systematic comparative evaluation across multiple dimensions: Comprehensive comparison of four feature types (CN, CNE, LM, BoW) across five classifiers (SVM-Linear, SVM-RBF, KNN, RF, Gaussian NB) and three datasets with different languages, narrative types, and text lengths provides broad empirical coverage.

Methodologically sound core idea: The adaptation of Perozzi et al. (2014) embedding enrichment to address the short-text problem is conceptually coherent and well-motivated by Amancio (2015c) observation that short texts produce linear networks with low topological informativeness.

Multilingual evaluation demonstrating cross-linguistic applicability: Testing on both English (DementiaBank) and Portuguese (Cinderella, ABCD) datasets with different narrative types provides evidence of generalization across languages and assessment contexts.

Transparent reporting of methodology and datasets: Clear description of network construction, feature extraction, classification algorithms, and detailed demographic information (Tables 1–3) enables reproducibility assessment and critical evaluation.

Competitive classification performance within baseline ranges: Reported accuracies (65–80%) fall within established baseline ranges (60–85%), suggesting the approach achieves competitive performance without requiring manual preprocessing or robust parsers.
limitations: Absence of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals is a critical methodological gap. No p-values, significance tests, or confidence intervals reported for any performance comparisons. With small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) and 5-fold cross-validation (resulting in 4–8 MCI samples per fold), reported performance differences may be within noise margins. This prevents reliable assessment of whether claimed improvements are statistically meaningful or due to random variation. Confidence in all comparative claims is substantially undermined.

Biased comparison between complex network and linguistic metric features: Linguistic metrics were pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features (constituency, dependency parsing) due to robustness concerns, while complex network features use all topological measures. This creates asymmetric comparison favoring CN. Additionally, Table 6 shows LM achieves 0.7250 (SVM-RBF) on manually cleaned Cinderella data versus CNE 0.6500, contradicting the main claim that CN outperforms LM. This result suggests that when linguistic metrics are properly preprocessed, they may outperform complex networks, undermining the paper's central argument.

Language-dependent threshold tuning directly contradicts language-independence claim: Embedding similarity thresholds differ between English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4) without justification or sensitivity analysis. The paper claims the approach is 'language-independent' (Abstract, Section 1) but requires language-specific parameter tuning. Additionally, different Coh-Metrix versions are used for different languages, and preprocessing differs (manual sentence segmentation in Cinderella, automatic in ABCD). These language-specific design choices undermine the language-independence narrative and suggest the approach is 'language-adaptable' rather than truly language-independent.

Disfluency robustness claimed but not directly tested: The paper asserts that complex networks are robust to disfluencies (Claim C4), but disfluencies were partially removed (filled pauses, false starts, repetitions) rather than fully preserved. No explicit comparison of performance on disfluent versus cleaned versions of the same dataset is provided. Disfluency handling is also inconsistent across datasets (automatic removal in Cookie Theft and Cinderella, automatic segmentation in ABCD). Without direct testing, the robustness claim remains unsubstantiated.
open_questions: Why do thresholds for embedding similarity differ between English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4)? What linguistic or statistical properties of these languages justify different thresholds? Would a language-independent threshold (e.g., 0.5) work equally well for both languages? Please provide sensitivity analysis showing accuracy across threshold range (0.1–0.9) for both languages.

How can the paper claim language-independence when threshold tuning, different Coh-Metrix versions, and preprocessing differ by language? Should the claim be revised to 'language-adaptable' rather than 'language-independent'? What aspects of the approach are truly language-independent versus language-dependent?

Why does Table 6 show linguistic metrics (LM 0.7250 SVM-RBF) outperforming enriched complex networks (CNE 0.6500 SVM-RBF) on manually cleaned Cinderella data? Does this contradict the main claim that complex networks outperform linguistic metrics? How should this result be interpreted?

How robust are complex networks to disfluencies? Please conduct explicit comparison of performance on disfluent versus cleaned versions of the same dataset (e.g., Cinderella). Which types of disfluencies (filled pauses, repetitions, revisions, paraphasias) most affect each feature type?

Are the reported performance differences statistically significant? Please conduct statistical significance testing (paired t-tests, McNemar's test) and report 95% confidence intervals for all accuracy values. With small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset), are the observed differences within noise margins?

Which topological features are most discriminative for MCI detection? What do these features reveal about language changes in MCI?

How do ensemble and multi-view learning weights affect performance? Please report multi-view learning weights explicitly and justify their selection. Why do improvements vary substantially across datasets (2.3% to 10%)? Is the majority voting strategy optimal, or would weighted voting or stacking perform better?
