consensus_snapshot: All five specialist reviewers identify absence of statistical significance testing as a major methodological gap that prevents reliable assessment of performance differences.
All reviewers note that linguistic metrics baseline is potentially biased by pre-filtering parser-dependent features, creating asymmetric comparison.
All reviewers identify language-dependent threshold tuning (0.7 vs 0.4) as contradicting language-independence claims.
All reviewers note that disfluency robustness is asserted but not directly tested via explicit comparison of disfluent versus cleaned versions.
All reviewers acknowledge the paper addresses a genuine clinical problem and proposes a methodologically sound core idea (embedding-enriched networks).
All reviewers recognize the systematic evaluation across multiple datasets and feature types as a strength.
All reviewers note small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) as limiting statistical power and generalizability.
disagreement_snapshot: Severity assessment of methodological gaps: Reviewers 1–2 (structure analyst, methodology auditor) treat statistical testing absence and biased comparison as disqualifying flaws; reviewers 3–4 (novelty assessors) view these as addressable limitations within incremental-contribution paradigm.

Interpretation of Table 6 result (LM 0.7250 vs CNE 0.6500 on clean Cinderella): Reviewers 1–2 cite as direct contradiction of main claim; reviewer 5 emphasizes as potential invalidation; reviewer 3 frames as confound rather than contradiction.

Language-independence claim: Reviewers 1–2 view language-dependent thresholds as direct contradiction; reviewer 4 suggests this may reflect legitimate language-specific optimization rather than fundamental limitation.

Disfluency robustness interpretation: Reviewers 1–2 emphasize claim is not directly tested; reviewer 4 suggests partial disfluency removal may be optimal strategy; reviewer 5 notes inconsistency but frames as incomplete testing rather than invalidation.

Novelty assessment: Reviewers 3–4 differ on whether application-level contribution (MCI detection) constitutes meaningful novelty versus incremental application of established techniques. Reviewer 3 (incremental lens) rates novelty as moderate; reviewer 4 (disruptive lens) rates as low.

Ensemble strategy evaluation: Reviewer 2 treats simplistic majority voting as methodological flaw; reviewer 4 suggests majority voting may be sufficient for this task; reviewer 5 notes inconsistent improvements (2.3–10%) as evidence of limited robustness.
uncertainty_snapshot: Statistical significance of performance differences: No significance testing reported. With small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) and 5-fold CV, confidence intervals for all accuracy claims are wide and unquantified. Reported differences (e.g., CNE 0.6264 vs LM 0.5806 on Cookie Theft) may be within noise margins.

Threshold selection justification: Different thresholds for English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4) lack justification. No sensitivity analysis provided. Unclear whether thresholds were optimized on test set (potential overfitting) or validation set. No evidence that language-independent threshold would not work equally well.

Linguistic metrics baseline fairness: LM features pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent metrics, while CN features use all topological measures. Comparison may be asymmetric. Table 6 contradicts main claim (LM 0.7250 > CNE 0.6500 on clean data). Unclear whether CN truly outperforms LM or whether pre-filtering biased comparison.

Disfluency robustness: Claim asserts robustness but disfluencies were partially removed (filled pauses, false starts) rather than fully preserved. No explicit comparison of disfluent vs. cleaned versions on same dataset. Inconsistent disfluency handling across datasets (manual segmentation in Cinderella, automatic in ABCD).

Age confound in ABCD: 11-year age difference between control (61) and MCI (72) groups. Age is known to affect language and cognitive performance. No stratified analysis or age-matching reported. Unclear whether high accuracy (80%) reflects MCI-specific patterns or age-related differences.

Embedding domain validation: Word embeddings trained with default parameters (Bojanowski et al. 2016) without domain-specific tuning or validation for medical/dementia language. No comparison with domain-specific embeddings. Unclear whether general-purpose embeddings capture medical/dementia-specific semantics.

Ensemble strategy robustness: Improvements inconsistent across datasets (2.3% to 10%). Majority voting is simplistic; no comparison with weighted voting or stacking. Multi-view learning weights not explicitly reported or optimized. Unclear whether improvements generalize or are dataset-specific.

Generalization scope: Evaluation limited to three datasets, two languages (English, Portuguese), and similar narrative tasks (Cookie Theft, Cinderella, ABCD). Generalization to other languages, assessment types, or MCI subtypes unclear. Results may be specific to Portuguese and English narratives.
source_trace: Amancio (2015c): Cited for observation that short texts produce linear networks with low topological informativeness; justifies embedding enrichment approach. Section 3 Modeling and Characterizing Texts.
Perozzi et al. (2014): Foundational work on enriching networks with word embeddings; approach adapted in this paper for MCI detection. Section 3 Modeling and Characterizing Texts.

Aluísio et al. (2016): Prior work on MCI detection from Portuguese Cinderella narratives using linguistic metrics; required manual preprocessing (disfluency removal, subject insertion). Motivates paper's approach to avoid manual preprocessing. Section 2 Related Work, Section 4.1.2, Table 6.

Bojanowski et al. (2016): FastText embeddings with character-level n-grams used for network enrichment. Trained with default parameters (100 dimensions, context window 5, 5 epochs) without domain-specific tuning. Section 4.2.1, Section 5.

Roark et al. (2011), Lehr et al. (2012), Tóth et al. (2015), Vincze et al. (2016): Prior work on MCI detection from speech; provide baseline accuracy range of 60–85%. Section 2 Related Work, Section 6 Conclusions.
DementiaBank (MacWhinney et al.): Source of English Cookie Theft dataset (43 MCI, 86 control). Section 4.1.1.
University of São Paulo Medical School: Source of Portuguese Cinderella (20 MCI, 20 control) and ABCD (23 MCI, 20 control) datasets. Section 4.1.2, Section 4.1.3.

Coh-Metrix (Graesser et al.): Linguistic feature extraction tool; 106 features for English, 58 metrics for Portuguese (Coh-Metrix-Dementia). Pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent features. Section 4.2.2.
DeepBond (Candido et al.): Automatic sentence segmentation method used for ABCD dataset. Section 4.1.3.
TalkBank guidelines: Disfluency removal guidelines followed for Cinderella dataset. Section 4.1.2.
transparency_notes: This meta-review synthesizes five specialist reviews operating under different cognitive roles (structure analyst, methodology auditor, incremental novelty assessor, disruptive novelty assessor, claim verifier) to provide comprehensive analytical coverage. Model diversity reveals tensions between novelty assessment and methodological rigor.
All reviewers identify lack of statistical significance testing as critical gap. Confidence in performance claims is substantially limited by absence of p-values and confidence intervals.

Biased comparison between CN and LM features is consistently identified across reviews. Table 6 result (LM 0.7250 > CNE 0.6500 on clean Cinderella) contradicts main claim and is flagged by multiple reviewers as requiring explanation.

Language-independence claim is contradicted by language-dependent threshold tuning (0.7 vs 0.4) and different Coh-Metrix versions. This contradiction is identified by all reviewers as requiring clarification or claim revision.

Disfluency robustness is asserted but not directly tested. Partial disfluency removal and inconsistent handling across datasets undermine robustness claims. Direct testing via disfluent vs. cleaned comparison is recommended by all reviewers.
Small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) with 5-fold CV result in high variance and unreliable estimates. Each fold contains only 4–8 MCI samples. Confidence in generalizability is low.

Age imbalance in ABCD dataset (11-year difference) is potential confound not addressed in analysis. Unclear whether high accuracy (80%) reflects MCI-specific patterns or age-related language differences.
Ensemble improvements are inconsistent across datasets (2.3–10%), suggesting limited robustness. Majority voting is simplistic; no comparison with weighted or other ensemble methods.
No feature importance analysis provided. All 30 topological features (10 metrics × 3 statistics) treated as black box. Mechanistic understanding of why networks work for MCI detection is lacking.
Comparison with baselines (60–85% range) is indirect due to different datasets and evaluation protocols. No head-to-head comparison on same dataset with same baseline methods.

Novelty assessment is complicated by tension between application-level contribution (MCI detection) and algorithmic innovation (limited). Different novelty lenses yield different conclusions about significance of contribution.

Retrieved literature corpus (Q1/Q2 articles) is limited. Absence of close matches does not imply lack of precedent in broader literature. Sparse coverage of clinical NLP applications may reflect indexing gaps rather than true novelty.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a novel application of embedding-enriched complex networks to MCI detection with pragmatic motivation and systematic evaluation, but exhibits significant methodological gaps that prevent strong conclusions about the superiority of the proposed approach. The core contribution—adapting Perozzi et al. (2014) embedding enrichment to short texts for MCI detection—is methodologically sound and addresses a genuine clinical bottleneck (avoiding manual preprocessing and parser-dependent feature extraction). However, empirical validation is underdeveloped. Critical concerns: (1) Absence of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals undermines all performance claims. With small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) and 5-fold CV, reported differences may be within noise margins. (2) Linguistic metrics baseline is weakened by pre-filtering parser-dependent features, creating asymmetric comparison. Table 6 result (LM 0.7250 vs CNE 0.6500 on clean Cinderella) contradicts main claim. (3) Language-dependent threshold tuning (0.7 vs 0.4) directly contradicts language-independence claim; no justification provided. (4) Disfluency robustness is asserted but not directly tested; disfluencies were partially removed rather than fully preserved. (5) Age imbalance in ABCD dataset (11-year difference) may confound results; no stratified analysis. (6) Ensemble improvements are inconsistent across datasets (2.3–10%), suggesting limited robustness. Recommendation: Desk reject or major revision required. If revision path is chosen, require: (a) Statistical significance testing with confidence intervals for all claims; (b) Fair comparison with linguistic metrics (either full feature set or equivalent filtering); (c) Sensitivity analysis for threshold selection across languages; (d) Explicit disfluency robustness testing (disfluent vs. cleaned versions); (e) Age-stratified analysis for ABCD; (f) Feature importance analysis to provide mechanistic understanding. The paper's practical motivation and systematic evaluation are strengths, but methodological rigor must be substantially improved before publication. Consider specialized venue (clinical NLP workshop, domain-specific conference) if major revision is not feasible.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper addresses a genuine clinical problem and proposes a reasonable methodological approach, but empirical validation requires substantial strengthening. To address reviewer concerns: (1) Conduct statistical significance testing (paired t-tests, McNemar's test) for all performance comparisons. Report 95% confidence intervals for all accuracy values. With small sample sizes, consider leave-one-out CV or stratified k-fold with larger k (e.g., 10-fold). (2) Provide fair comparison with linguistic metrics: either use full Coh-Metrix feature sets without pre-filtering, or apply equivalent filtering to both CN and LM features. Explain why Table 6 shows LM outperforming CNE on clean Cinderella data (0.7250 vs 0.6500). (3) Justify threshold selection: provide sensitivity analysis showing accuracy across threshold range (0.1–0.9) for both English and Portuguese. Explain why different thresholds are optimal for different languages, or demonstrate that language-independent threshold works equally well. (4) Directly test disfluency robustness: evaluate on both disfluent and cleaned versions of same dataset (e.g., Cinderella). Report results separately for each version. Analyze which disfluency types most affect each feature type. (5) Address age confound in ABCD: report results stratified by age group or use age-matched control group. Include age as covariate in classification model. (6) Validate word embeddings for medical/dementia domain: compare general-purpose embeddings with domain-specific embeddings trained on medical corpora. (7) Conduct ablation study isolating contribution of embedding enrichment: vary threshold, compare with alternative enrichment methods, analyze which topological features benefit most from enrichment. (8) Analyze ensemble robustness: investigate why improvements vary across datasets (2.3–10%). Compare majority voting with weighted voting and stacking. Report multi-view learning weights explicitly. (9) Provide feature importance analysis: identify which topological metrics are most discriminative for MCI detection. Interpret findings in terms of language/cognitive properties. (10) Revise claims to match evidence: acknowledge language-dependent parameter tuning; frame as 'language-adaptable' rather than 'language-independent'. Acknowledge that disfluency handling is partial rather than complete. Clarify that ensemble improvements are inconsistent across datasets. Consider submitting to specialized venue (clinical NLP workshop, neuropsychological assessment conference) if major revision is not feasible.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes enriching word co-occurrence networks with word embeddings to detect mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from speech transcripts. The core methodological contribution—adapting Perozzi et al. (2014) embedding enrichment to address the short-text problem—is sound and novel in application. The paper provides systematic evaluation across three multilingual datasets (English DementiaBank, Portuguese Cinderella, Portuguese ABCD), four feature types (CN, CNE, LM, BoW), and five classifiers. Reported accuracies (65–80%) fall within established baseline ranges (60–85%). The practical motivation is genuine: avoiding manual preprocessing and parser-dependent feature extraction for disfluent clinical speech. However, empirical validation is underdeveloped and several key claims are overstated relative to available evidence.

Strengths:
- Pragmatic motivation addressing genuine clinical bottleneck: The paper identifies a real problem in neuropsychological assessment (expensive manual preprocessing) and proposes a lightweight, parser-free alternative grounded in prior work (Aluísio et al. 2016).
- Systematic comparative evaluation: Comprehensive comparison of four feature types across five classifiers and three datasets with different languages and narrative types provides broad empirical coverage.
- Methodologically sound core idea: Adaptation of Perozzi et al. (2014) embedding enrichment to address short-text problem is conceptually coherent and well-motivated by Amancio (2015c) observation.
- Multilingual evaluation: Testing on English and Portuguese datasets with different narrative types provides evidence of cross-linguistic applicability.
- Transparent reporting: Clear methodology description and detailed demographic information enable reproducibility assessment.
- Competitive performance: Reported accuracies (65–80%) within baseline ranges (60–85%) suggest the approach achieves competitive performance without manual preprocessing.

Limitations:
- Absence of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals is critical methodological gap. No p-values, significance tests, or confidence intervals reported for any performance comparisons. With small sample sizes (20–43 MCI per dataset) and 5-fold CV (4–8 MCI per fold), reported differences may be within noise margins. Confidence in all comparative claims is substantially undermined.
- Biased comparison between complex network and linguistic metric features: LM features pre-filtered to exclude parser-dependent metrics, while CN features use all topological measures. This creates asymmetric comparison. Additionally, Table 6 shows LM 0.7250 (SVM-RBF) on clean Cinderella versus CNE 0.6500, contradicting main claim that CN outperforms LM. This suggests that when LM is properly preprocessed, it may outperform CN, undermining the paper's central argument.
- Language-dependent threshold tuning directly contradicts language-independence claim: Embedding similarity thresholds differ between English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4) without justification or sensitivity analysis. Paper claims 'language-independent' approach but requires language-specific parameter tuning. Different Coh-Metrix versions and inconsistent preprocessing (manual vs. automatic segmentation) further undermine language-independence narrative.
- Disfluency robustness claimed but not directly tested: Paper asserts robustness to disfluencies but disfluencies were partially removed (filled pauses, false starts) rather than fully preserved. No explicit comparison of disfluent versus cleaned versions on same dataset. Inconsistent disfluency handling across datasets prevents assessment of robustness.

Open Questions:
- Why do thresholds for embedding similarity differ between English (0.7) and Portuguese (0.4)? What linguistic or statistical properties justify different thresholds? Would language-independent threshold work equally well? Please provide sensitivity analysis across threshold range (0.1–0.9) for both languages.
- How can the paper claim language-independence when threshold tuning, different Coh-Metrix versions, and preprocessing differ by language? Should claim be revised to 'language-adaptable'? What aspects are truly language-independent versus language-dependent?
- Why does Table 6 show LM (0.7250 SVM-RBF) outperforming CNE (0.6500 SVM-RBF) on clean Cinderella data? Does this contradict main claim? How should this result be interpreted?
- How robust are complex networks to disfluencies? Please conduct explicit comparison of disfluent versus cleaned versions of same dataset. Which disfluency types most affect each feature type?
- Are reported performance differences statistically significant? Please conduct significance testing and report confidence intervals. With small sample sizes, are observed differences within noise margins?
- Which topological features are most discriminative for MCI detection? Please conduct feature importance analysis to identify which of 30 features drive classification. What do these features reveal about language changes in MCI?
- How do ensemble and multi-view learning weights affect performance? Please report weights explicitly. Why do improvements vary substantially across datasets (2.3–10%)? Is majority voting optimal?
- Is age a confounding variable in ABCD dataset? 11-year age difference between control (61) and MCI (72) is substantial. Please report results stratified by age or use age-matched group. Does age explain higher accuracy (80%) on ABCD?

Transparency:
The paper clearly documents preprocessing steps, dataset characteristics, and demographic information, enabling reproducibility assessment. Methodology is generally well-described with clear explanations of network construction and feature extraction. Results are presented comprehensively in Tables 4–7. However, the paper does not report confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests, limiting interpretability of performance differences. The paper acknowledges some limitations (e.g., comparison with baselines is not straightforward) but does not fully address implications. Transparency gap exists between claims (language-independence, robustness to disfluencies) and evidence (language-dependent thresholds, partial disfluency removal). The paper does not provide code or data availability statements, limiting reproducibility.

The study by Vanunu et al. [ 49] applied a diffusion- based method named PRINCE to prioritize genes in pros- tate cancer, AD and type 2 diabetes. What underpins these key research studies and future studies is the reliance on human interactome maps which are critical to the understanding of genotype-phenotype relationships [ 37]. In this study, we aim into investigate whether experimental data or curated data used to construct a human protein–protein interaction network (PPIN) has an impact upon disease network analysis. Using our previously proposed integrative network-driven pipeline [ 5] we integrate diverse heterogeneous data including: gene-expression, PPIN, ontology-based simi- larity, degree connectivity and betweenness centrality measures to uncover potential disease-candidate genes. To investigate the effect of human PPIN selection, a com- parison of disease-gene candidates is presented when different human PPINs are integrated into the framework. Two PPINs have been selected for this study: (1) the recently published proteome-scale map of the Human Interactome Network by Rolland et al. [ 37] which is referred to as PPIN_HTP and (2) a literature curated map obtained from extracting binary PPIs from public data- bases referred to as PPIN_LIT [ 51]. Content: As a counter to common problems with reviews, there are also common problems with NLP papers. We do ask you to watch out for these and point them out when you see them. top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Rejer ( &) Faculty of Computer Science, West Pomeranian University of Technology, Szczecin, Zolnierska 49, 71-210 Szczecin, Poland e-mail: irejer@wi.zut.edu.pl 123 Pattern Anal Applic (2015) 18:485–492 DOI 10.1007/s10044-014-0425-3 costs of implementing the BCI, and above all—higher comfort for its user. There are three main groups of feature selection meth- ods [ 4, 5]: ﬁlters, wrappers and embedded methods. The characteristic feature of the methods from the ﬁrst group is that they have no connection with the classiﬁcation pro- cess. Hence, to use them, a classiﬁer is not needed. Some popular methods from this group are [ 6, 7]: Information Gain, ReliefF, Correlation-based Feature Selection (CFS), and Consistency-based Feature Selection. On the contrary to the ﬁlters, wrappers and embedded methods need a classiﬁer. While wrappers use a classiﬁer only to evaluate succeeding feature subsets, embedded methods perform the selection as an inner process during the classiﬁer training. The commonly used methods from both groups are: step- wise selection [ 8, 9], genetic algorithms [ 10] and random selection [ 11] (wrappers) and Recursive Feature Elimina- tion [ 12], elastic net [ 13], and LASSO [ 14] (embedded methods). The study by Vanunu et al. [ 49] applied a diffusion- based method named PRINCE to prioritize genes in pros- tate cancer, AD and type 2 diabetes. What underpins these key research studies and future studies is the reliance on human interactome maps which are critical to the understanding of genotype-phenotype relationships [ 37]. In this study, we aim into investigate whether experimental data or curated data used to construct a human protein–protein interaction network (PPIN) has an impact upon disease network analysis. Using our previously proposed integrative network-driven pipeline [ 5] we integrate diverse heterogeneous data including: gene-expression, PPIN, ontology-based simi- larity, degree connectivity and betweenness centrality measures to uncover potential disease-candidate genes. To investigate the effect of human PPIN selection, a com- parison of disease-gene candidates is presented when different human PPINs are integrated into the framework. Two PPINs have been selected for this study: (1) the recently published proteome-scale map of the Human Interactome Network by Rolland et al. [ 37] which is referred to as PPIN_HTP and (2) a literature curated map obtained from extracting binary PPIs from public data- bases referred to as PPIN_LIT [ 51]. There are three main groups of feature selection meth- ods [ 4, 5]: ﬁlters, wrappers and embedded methods. The characteristic feature of the methods from the ﬁrst group is that they have no connection with the classiﬁcation pro- cess. Hence, to use them, a classiﬁer is not needed. Some popular methods from this group are [ 6, 7]: Information Gain, ReliefF, Correlation-based Feature Selection (CFS), and Consistency-based Feature Selection. On the contrary to the ﬁlters, wrappers and embedded methods need a classiﬁer. While wrappers use a classiﬁer only to evaluate succeeding feature subsets, embedded methods perform the selection as an inner process during the classiﬁer training. top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

There are three main groups of feature selection meth- ods [ 4, 5]: ﬁlters, wrappers and embedded methods. The characteristic feature of the methods from the ﬁrst group is that they have no connection with the classiﬁcation pro- cess. Hence, to use them, a classiﬁer is not needed. Some popular methods from this group are [ 6, 7]: Information Gain, ReliefF, Correlation-based Feature Selection (CFS), and Consistency-based Feature Selection. On the contrary to the ﬁlters, wrappers and embedded methods need a classiﬁer. While wrappers use a classiﬁer only to evaluate succeeding feature subsets, embedded methods perform the selection as an inner process during the classiﬁer training. The commonly used methods from both groups are: step- wise selection [ 8, 9], genetic algorithms [ 10] and random selection [ 11] (wrappers) and Recursive Feature Elimina- tion [ 12], elastic net [ 13], and LASSO [ 14] (embedded methods).
